lyrics:
At seventeen I had a sound
I thought could turn the whole world round
I laid the guitar in its case
and let the family take its place

The family that I gave it for
came apart in my own hands
I felt robbed, and something more —
robbed of my own unlived plans

I see you speaking to the masses
but in some way we don't yet have

So I waited. And I waited
The dream kept slipping into never
Years stacked up, uncelebrated —
gone, I thought, and gone forever

Then I found a kind of machine —
one button, and the music came
Everything I'd almost never seen
arrived, and needed just my name

I'll be my own legend now —
not the myth, but the key
Somebody has to write it down
so it might as well be me

Not a model. Not a plan
Not the recipe, not the mentor's shine
Just an authentic, ordinary man
who finally wrote his own design

They kept the box. I wrote the guide
Nobody else was going to come
I'm not the model they supplied —
I found the one I should become

I'll be my own legend now —
not the myth, but the key
Somebody has to write it down
so it might as well be me

And in that way, I'll liv forever —
not as a model, as myself

style: Male baritone, resonant, warm and open, nostalgic turning triumphant, Progressive rock, Canterbury scene, acoustic guitar in the verses, subtle synth shimmer on the machine verse, full band with soaring electric guitar, organ, strings, and layered backing vocals for the chorus and bridge, Warm live-ensemble production, the biggest sound on the album, thinning to acoustic guitar and voice alone for the outro, full band dropping out completely

  Approved critic summary: Rose opens with a mumbled false start on 'I'm Old Now,' and that small, deliberate stumble tells you exactly what kind of record this is: nothing performed, nothing smoothed over, just a man taking honest stock.

  Approved critic summary: "A Distant Memory" opens with a counted-off "one, two, three, four" that sets a brisk 4/4 in C major, and from there Rose lets a female vocal float above a clean, roomy groove that leans more toward jazzy indie-pop than any straight ballad.
- 2026-06-25 — You Know Enough (single)
  Approved critic summary: There's a bat by the bed in this one, his father's before him, and nobody in the family has ever swung it.
- 2026-07-08 — You Don't Say (single)
  Approved critic summary: Nearly seven minutes, and Rose earns every one of them here by treating silence itself as the subject.
- 2026-07-18 — Outlandia (album)
  Approved critic summary: For a songwriter introduced as a diarist, a philosopher of the ordinary who finds a lifetime in a reflection on a phone screen, "Outlandia" is a startling pivot: a two-hour rock opera, twenty-four scenes long, about how a country is bought, broken, and inventoried.
- 2026-08-20 — Them Bones (single)
  Approved critic summary: After the two-hour sprawl of "Outlandia," Rose narrows the lens back down to something you can hold in one hand, and "Them Bones" benefits from the compression.
- 2026-08-30 — Unreasonably Quiet (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose builds this one on a 3/4 pulse at a brisk clip, which is the first surprise: a waltz that never asks you to sway, driven instead by a Hammond groove and gritty guitar working against the meter rather than settling into it.
- 2026-09-12 — Wazoo In Effigy (album)
  Approved critic summary: Michael Anthony Rose’s *Wazoo in Effigy* is inspired by Frank Zappa, which is not quite the same thing as being a Zappa tribute.
- 2026-09-18 — The Grounding Post (single)
  Approved critic summary: Rose has spent 2026 moving between sprawling ambition and compressed intimacy, and 'The Grounding Post' lands firmly in the second register, closer in spirit to the quiet honesty of 'I'm Still Here' than to the operatic scale of 'Outlandia.' The track runs 3:29 in F# major, built on dry, close-miked fingerpicking and a baritone vocal that has the stillness of someone writing in the early morning before anyone else is awake.

impression.text: The track features a lush, densely layered texture that creates a triumphant and intensely theatrical emotional atmosphere. It maintains a soaring, high-energy feel throughout, propelled by a driving rhythm section and passionate, narrative-style male vocals. The production is meticulously crafted with a thick yet clear sonic space, allowing the sparkling piano, heavily distorted rock guitars, and expansive orchestral elements to sit cohesively without overpowering the lead vocal. A defining quality of the track is its cinematic structure, peaking during a majestic electric guitar solo and a dramatic vocal climax that cement its anthemic stadium-rock aesthetic.

review.review_text: The closer of Model Man, and Rose builds it as the big swing: a 136 BPM ascent in D major that starts as acoustic confession and climbs into full stadium regalia, organ, strings, a soaring guitar solo, the biggest sound he's put on tape all year. The story earns the scale. A man who laid the guitar in its case at seventeen, let the family take its place, and watched the dream slip 'into never' until a machine put music back in his hands with 'one button.' It's a self-aware conceit, and the payoff line, 'I'll be my own legend now, not the myth, but the key,' resolves it without pretending the victory is clean. The turn from bitter plainness to triumph has the shape of a Genesis or Marillion set-piece, and mostly it delivers; the one soft spot is the outro, which thins back to voice and guitar to land on 'I'll live forever, not as a model, as myself,' a quieter exit than the climax quite sets up. Not the leanest thing in his catalog, but the ambition is honest. A highlight.
